Ty the Tasmanian Tiger est un jeu vidéo développé et édité par Krome Studios en 2002 pour GameCube, PlayStation 2 et Xbox. Le titre bénéficie finalement d'un portage sur Windows en fin d'année 2016.

Le titre se présente comme un jeu de plateformes en trois dimensions orienté vers l’exploration et la collecte, caractéristique des productions du début des années 2000. L’action se déroule dans un univers inspiré de l’Australie, mêlant espaces naturels et zones habitées. Le joueur incarne Ty, un tigre de Tasmanie anthropomorphe, chargé de retrouver des talismans afin de libérer sa famille et de mettre un terme aux ambitions de l’antagoniste Boss Cass.

Le jeu s’organise autour d’une structure semi-ouverte. Un point central permet d’accéder à différents niveaux, chacun proposant une série d’objectifs : collecte d’objets, défis annexes et exploration libre. La progression repose sur l’accumulation de ces éléments, ce qui incite à revisiter les zones pour atteindre une complétion totale.

Le système de jeu repose en grande partie sur l’utilisation de boomerangs. Ceux-ci remplissent à la fois un rôle offensif et utilitaire. Plusieurs variantes sont progressivement accessibles (feu, glace, électricité), chacune apportant des propriétés spécifiques. Cette mécanique introduit une certaine diversité, bien que son exploitation reste globalement simple.

La prise en main se montre accessible et adaptée à un large public. Les phases de plateformes privilégient la lisibilité et la fluidité plutôt que la difficulté. Les affrontements restent basiques et ne constituent pas l’élément central de l’expérience.

Sur le plan technique, le jeu propose une direction artistique colorée et cohérente, fortement marquée par son inspiration australienne. Les environnements se montrent variés et facilement identifiables. L’ambiance sonore, notamment à travers les musiques et les accents, participe à l’identité du titre. Toutefois, les animations et la modélisation reflètent les standards de leur époque.

Certaines limites apparaissent néanmoins sur la durée. La répétition des objectifs peut affecter le rythme de progression, et la caméra manque parfois de précision dans les phases de plateformes. Par ailleurs, le niveau de difficulté reste modéré, ce qui peut réduire l’intérêt pour les joueurs en quête de défi.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger se distingue comme une expérience de plateformes accessible et cohérente, reposant sur des bases solides mais classiques. Il privilégie le confort de jeu et l’exploration à la complexité mécanique, offrant une aventure agréable mais peu exigeante.

[h1]Succès Steam[/h1]

Les succès s’inscrivent dans la logique du jeu, en mettant l’accent sur la collecte et l’exploration complète des niveaux. Obtenir le 100 % demande de revisiter chaque zone afin de récupérer l’ensemble des objets et de remplir tous les objectifs. L’ensemble reste accessible, sans exigence technique élevée, mais requiert méthode et patience.

[h1]Pour résumer :[/h1]

✔️[u]Points positifs :[/u]

*Une direction artistique colorée et cohérente.
*Un univers original et identifiable.
*Une mécanique de boomerangs efficace.
*Une accessibilité adaptée à un large public.

❌[u]Points négatifs :[/u]

*Une répétitivité des objectifs.
*Une difficulté limitée.
*Une caméra parfois imprécise.
*Un manque de profondeur globale.

This is a case where I wish Steam had a mixed option. Despite the fact that I'm gonna have a lot of negative things to say regarding this game. I want to specify upfront that Ty the Tasmanian Tiger is a solid 3D platformer that I recommend to any fans of 3D platformers, but not a game I can wholly recommend outside of that demographic.

Before I criticize this game lets start with that I liked
-The Presentation. 
I don't so much mean the cutscenes, because those are pretty wooden (not necessarily a problem for me, I don't expect Jak and Daxter animation from a B-grade platformer). I more so mean the art design. I think Ty honestly looks really good for its time, and still (largely) holds up today from an art design POV. I think this game captures the Australian outback setting really well, and the game in general is just pretty to look at if you ask me. Although I called the cutscene animation wooden, I think the character models are actually pretty great for the most part. They aren't the most expressive, but for a B grade platformer these character models are honestly well above average, I think the character models in this game look better than the character models from Sly Cooper 1, and I wouldnt call that a B grade platformer.

-The controls (mostly) & general gameplay feel
Ty the tasmanian tiger has excellent controls. Ty is responsive to inputs, the boomerangs feel great to use, and I largely feel in control. Ty isn't a high movement tech type of platformer, it's much more about exploration. At first the camera really annoyed me because it was heavily zoomed in and I found the FOV to be completely horrible, it was nearly unplayable. Thankfully you can zoom the camera out (RB on Xbox Controller, C/Mouse wheel if you play with M&KB) however I dont remember if the game tells you this, and for the first three worlds of the game I was not remotely enjoying my time playing this game. Speaking of M&KB, this game plays shockingly well with that set-up and tbh, I preferred playing this game on M&KB because I thought the camera control was 10-fold better. The camera isn't necessarily horrible on controller, it just feels simultaneously over sensitive, and under sensitive. Meanwhile using my mouse to control the camera felt perfect. Like I said earlier, Ty isn't about precise platforming, it's about exploration, so I think that's why this game plays shockingly well on M&KB.

-The Music
I don't have much to say here, Ty just has really good music. There's great variety, it's catchy, and it's just an all around great soundtrack

Now onto why this game didn’t gel with me as much as I wanted it to
-Ty 1 just feels like a lot of what I’ve played before
Ty 1 is undoubtedly inspired by the likes of its collect-a-thon contemporaries of the time, mainly Banjo Kazooie and the Spyro trilogy. Unfortunately, I just don’t think Ty from a gameplay perspective really does anything to stand apart from those games, as such I just wish I was playing either of those games. Like if we’re talking exploration, I think Banjo Kazooie is superior because the levels are much more compact, and there’s less dead space in that game compared to this one. When compared to Spyro, what I said about Banjo can apply there as well, but I think Spyro has vastly superior gameplay pacing compared to Ty 1. For starters, even at his default speed Spyro moves a lot faster than Ty does, but Spyro also has his charge which makes going through levels faster and improves the gameplay pacing drastically. Ty has no way to speed himself up, his default movement speed isn’t the worst, in a vacuum. However with how ridiculously large some of these levels can get towards the back half of the game, it’s unbearably slow at points. I think a simple fix for this would’ve been a dash button to let Ty run on all 4s, but as a means of balancing it for combat, maybe you’d have to come out of the dash so you can start fighting, or if you’re good enough you could just stay in the dash and try to avoid enemy encounters. I think this would give Ty 1 a nice risk vs reward element. I digress, but suffice to say, from a gameplay POV, I don’t think Ty is doing enough to stand out amongst its contemporaries. If we’re gonna look at J&D (precursor legacy only) that game was doing a seamless open world & connecting everything together as a means of immersing you in the games world. If we look at R&C, that game had a heavy focus on combat & satarized consumerism with its writing, and Sly 1, it had a heavy emphasis on story-telling paired with its stealth theming. I’m aware Sly & Ratchet were a bit too new at the time, but that doesn’t change the fact that I feel like Ty 1 failed to stand out from a gameplay POV amongst contemporary platformers.

-Ty 1 kinda has an identity crisis with the type of game it wants to be
Ty 1 can’t decide rather it wants to be a linear point A to point B platformer, or a huge open ended collect-a-thon. It kinda flip flops between the levels. Like walk in the park is fairly linear with a few off-beat paths, then the following level Ship-Rex is an open ended level where you traverse the entire map into multiple areas. I think the problem with this is that the levels that are linear are largely superior to the open ended levels, and it goes back to what I said about Ty’s default movement speed paired with how large the open ended levels are. The linear levels I think have fantastic pacing, meanwhile the open ended levels fall into the dead space trapping I mentioned earlier. Like the open ended levels can just have so much dead level design that looks the same, so its difficult to navigate. It also leads into what I call the “Where’s that last collectible” issue that a lot of collect-a-thon games can suffer from (but to be fair the linear levels aren’t free of this either). I really wish Ty 1 had something like Sparx from the Spyro games, something that can point out gems (or in this game’s case Egg Orbs). Maybe do something like press a button with the Sonar rangs out and it’ll point you in a general direction without outright telling you where the item is unless you’re right next to it. I can already hear the argument that exploration is the main selling point of Ty/this genre of games as a whole. Respectfully however, I don’t think the Sparx mechanic from the Spyro games ruins the exploration aspect of those games and if anything only serves as a means to improve the game and keep it moving. In conclusion, this game fluctuates heavily in quality on a level by level basis, with the linear levels being superior to the open ended levels, exception being Outback Safari because that’s my favorite level in the game

-Ty 1 just loses steam the longer it goes on
I unfortunately find that Ty 1 kinda wears thin by the time its all said and done. It’s a mix of, the level themes start to get re-used so it feels like the game is running out of ideas, the combat hardly evolves so you just start avoiding enemies more than anything, every level has virtually the same set-up so it gets kinda repetitive (not unique to this game admittedly, but it stands out more because after a certain point I just grow tired). Ty 1 I think has a strong start but due to my aforementioned issues, this game just becomes kinda mind-numbing near the end. There are some great levels near the end, I particularly like Bridge on the river Ty. However I just find the weakest levels are in the back-half of the game, and the finale gauntlet is seriously one of the most ant-climatic finales in any game I’ve ever played.

-Concluding thoughts
Ty 1 is an aight game, but I can't recommend it on the whole. I think this is the right game for the right crowd, but because I just feel like there's more engaging platformers out there, I'm marking this as not recommended, even if I kinda like the game. Really wish Steam had a mixed feelings option because that more accurately sums up my thoughts on this game :/

Classic 3D Platformer

TY the Tasmanian Tiger, developed and published by Krome Studios, is a colorful 3D platformer that captures the spirit of the early 2000s collect-a-thon era while carving out its own identity through distinctly Australian flavor and heartfelt charm. At its core, the game follows Ty, the last of the Tasmanian Tigers, on a quest to rescue his family from the mysterious Dreaming by collecting magical Thunder Eggs scattered across a wide range of semi-open environments. The premise is simple and archetypal—hero sets out to save loved ones and restore balance—but it is delivered with warmth and personality that make the journey memorable rather than generic.

The structure revolves around hub-based progression, with interconnected areas leading to themed levels that range from coastal beaches and dense bushland to snowy mountains and arid outback plains. Each level emphasizes exploration, encouraging players to scour every corner for Thunder Eggs, hidden bilbies, golden cogs, and thousands of collectible opals. Unlike more linear platformers, the stages often feel like contained playgrounds, blending light platforming challenges with combat encounters and small mission objectives. Some tasks involve racing against the clock, others revolve around defeating specific enemies or solving environmental puzzles. This variety keeps the core loop engaging and prevents the collect-a-thon design from feeling monotonous.

A defining feature of the experience is Ty’s arsenal of boomerangs. Far more than a simple ranged attack, these boomerangs introduce mechanical diversity throughout the adventure. Frost boomerangs freeze enemies and water surfaces, flame boomerangs ignite obstacles, and other specialized variants open up creative interactions with the environment. Combat remains accessible and straightforward—throwing boomerangs at quirky enemies and dodging their attacks—but the variety in tools adds a satisfying layer of experimentation. The progression of unlocking new boomerangs gives a sense of steady empowerment, allowing earlier levels to be revisited with new capabilities and secrets uncovered.

Tonally, the game radiates charm. The characters speak with playful Australian slang, and the supporting cast—ranging from inventive scientists to mischievous antagonists—adds a whimsical layer to the adventure. The humor is light and family-friendly, often leaning into caricature without becoming mean-spirited. Visually, the bright color palette and stylized character designs maintain a timeless cartoon quality that ages more gracefully than many early 3D titles. The environments, though technically simple by modern standards, are vibrant and distinct enough to create a strong sense of place. Combined with an upbeat soundtrack that evokes the relaxed yet adventurous feel of the outback, the presentation remains one of the game’s strongest assets.

That said, its early 2000s origins are still evident in certain aspects of design. The camera can occasionally struggle in tighter spaces, and platforming precision does not always match contemporary expectations. Some missions feel repetitive, particularly when collecting large quantities of opals without a streamlined tracking system. These limitations reflect the design conventions of its era rather than outright flaws, but modern players may notice moments where controls feel slightly less refined than today’s genre leaders. However, these issues rarely overshadow the overall enjoyment, especially once players acclimate to the movement and pacing.

The Steam release and subsequent updates have helped modernize the experience with improved visuals, smoother performance, and controller support, making it far more accessible on contemporary systems. Nostalgia undoubtedly plays a role in its enduring popularity, yet even newcomers can appreciate its approachable design and cheerful tone. Unlike many platformers that rely heavily on difficulty spikes, TY maintains a relatively balanced challenge level, making it inviting for players of varying skill levels while still offering optional completionist goals for those who want to gather every collectible.

Ultimately, TY the Tasmanian Tiger stands as a testament to a particular era of platforming where exploration, personality, and imaginative tools defined the experience. It does not aim to reinvent the genre, but it succeeds in delivering a cohesive, charming adventure that remains enjoyable decades after its debut. For players who value colorful worlds, inventive gadget-based progression, and a lighthearted tone grounded in unique cultural flavor, it offers a satisfying journey that feels both nostalgic and enduringly heartfelt.

TY the Tasmanian Tiger is a game I had never played back in the day. I was in the mood for a 3D platforming collect-a-thon, and TY the Tasmanian Tiger is definitely that. Is it the best 3D platformer of all time? Not even close. But it's a decent enough game with a lot of charm. I really enjoyed the characters, enemies, and boomerang action gameplay. 

I did run into a bug right on the first level where I couldn't collect everything until I exited and re-entered the level, but that was the only time that happened. The game is a little rough in some spots. Hit detection can be wonky. Sometimes you think you're doing something the right way, but the game just doesn't register it because of the hitboxes, and so you end up trying something else until you realize the game was just being weird and you were doing it right all along. There was one puzzle where the solution was something that didn't work in a different level, so I didn't even bother trying it.

Some things feel...err...heavily inspired by other games. There a number of comparisons I could make to Banjo-Kazooie, from the sound of collecting cogs to the bilbies feeling really similar to Jinjos. 

Each level has a sort of Mario 64 style set of objectives, one of which is collecting all 300 opals in each level. The levels and hub area don't feel quite as fleshed out as in Mario 64 or Banjo Kazooie, but it gets the job done. If you've played all the classics, Ty has plenty of fun to be had, but it's more of a B-tier game in the grand scheme of things.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger comes from the era of sixth-gen mascot puzzle platformers, back when that was what a good chunk of the industry was focused on. Its level based collectathon, with a surprisingly open ended approach. Its gimmick is that it has Australian set dressing, with boomerangs as weapons. With a fairly generic (but fun) cast of voiced wacky characters, you explore various locations in Australia to collect some mystic talismans, and stop Boss Cass, the cassowary antagonist who imprisoned his parents in some sub-dimension. Standard stuff for the era, really aimed for the preteen audience. 

But, since its a game of its era, the protagonist is a generically upbeat tasmanian tiger, who wears swim trunks everywhere. The game is remarkably easy, and yet sometimes the jumps can feel slightly unfair and inconsistent. Your moveset is fairly limited. You are given two boomerangs early on, not just for an offensive boost, but because this allows you to glide. For the most part you interact with the world with a really poor gun, otherwise Ty can jump, bite and glide. In certain instances he can chain bites, and this is used to scale a chains of floating spy cameras (???), to reach new areas. Its used in most of the levels, but never in a way that is clever or innovative. The auto aiming system for the boomerangs and the bites is imprecise, and the platforming at times feels inconsistent, at least at first, but by the time I understand the aiming and movement system the game is over.

It feels like a game that is at best an iteration on Mario 64, something that plays very similar to the first Sly cooper game. Both games came out in 2002, and both games were still experimenting with the formula. However Ty was a game that was really trying to create a more open world experience. The game is a series of linear levels that are clustered around one elemental theme, with three levels that you can tackle in any order. After getting enough resources, you fight a boss, and get a new elemental boomerang that solves a simple puzzle. Like a fire boomerang that will burn some webs, or an Ice boomerang that freezes water to make a bridge. Nothing radically innovative, but if it is your jam then you already probably know about it.

So why would anyone new play it now, outside of nostalgia, or historical curiosity? Well there are ton of interesting ideas and gameplay decisions. You can view it as not only what the industry was doing at the time, but also how game design has changed. The Aussie coat of paint is unique, and genuine. The mad max dressed frill lizards, our “goomba” in this game, is extremely well done. The levels have multiple branching paths, and reward exploration better than most games of the era. Most of your progress is gated by collectibles that you can get from anywhere. So you never even have to do the intended main mission on any map and you can still complete the entire game. The boomerangs are varied, and have interesting abilities. However, they are criminally underutilized. Most boomerangs never need to be used, since they are all optional, which puts the onus on the gated “elemental rangs”. The core problem is there are only around 10 elemental puzzles in the entire game. 

I recommend it over most of the other mascot puzzle platformer of the time, not because its the best of its era, but because it captures what a certain subsection of mainstream gaming was like at the time. It being still fun is just a bonus.

Mate… this isn’t just a game, this is a straight-up time machine in disc form. Booting up TY the Tasmanian Tiger doesn’t just take me back to my childhood—it dropkicks me through a portal straight into the early 2000s, where life was simpler, controllers had wires, and every mascot platformer was trying to outshine Crash and Spyro.

TY wasn’t just another furry mascot—he was Australia’s answer to gaming greatness. Dual boomerangs? Iconic. That cheesy-but-charming Aussie accent? Legendary. Collecting opals and snagging Thunder Eggs? Peak dopamine. Every level drips with charm: from lush rainforests to outback deserts, this game gave us some of the most vibrant, personality-packed worlds of its era.

The gameplay? Tight, fun, and creative. Every new boomerang upgrade made me feel like I was unlocking god-tier powers, even if it was just freezing water or setting enemies on fire. And the characters? Pure Saturday morning cartoon energy. Shazza, Sly, Boss Cass—they’re burned into my brain forever.

And let’s not forget that soundtrack. Absolute banger. Those didgeridoo-infused tunes still live rent-free in my head, and hearing them again hits me harder than any triple-A nostalgia cash grab ever could.

Revisiting TY today feels like hugging your childhood best friend—you instantly remember why you loved them, flaws and all. It wasn’t about being the “best platformer ever,” it was about heart, personality, and pure fun. TY stood proud in a sea of mascots, and for me? He still does.
